title: How Helmet Laws in Michigan Impact Your Motorcycle Claim
author: barrixlaw
contentHtml:
Motorcycle accidents can lead to devastating injuries, and understanding Michigan’s helmet laws is crucial when filing an injury claim. If you’ve been involved in a crash, the use—or non-use—of a helmet can significantly impact your legal case. This article explores how Michigan’s helmet laws influence motorcycle accident claims and why hiring a Motorcycle Accident Lawyer in Michigan is essential for protecting your rights.

Understanding Michigan’s Helmet Laws

Michigan’s helmet law has undergone significant changes over the years. As of 2012, the state allows certain motorcyclists to ride without a helmet under specific conditions. According to Michigan Compiled Laws (MCL) 257.658, riders who meet the following requirements can legally ride without a helmet:

  • They must be at least 21 years old.
  • They must carry at least $20,000 in medical insurance coverage.
  • If operating a motorcycle with a passenger, the passenger must also meet these requirements.
  • They must have held a motorcycle endorsement for at least two years or have completed an approved motorcycle safety course.

However, riders under 21 years old must wear a Department of Transportation (DOT)-approved helmet at all times.

How Helmet Use Affects Motorcycle Injury Claims

1. Comparative Negligence in Michigan

Michigan follows a comparative negligence rule, meaning that the compensation you receive can be reduced based on your level of fault. If you were not wearing a helmet at the time of the accident, the at-fault party’s insurance company may argue that your injuries were worsened due to your choice not to wear protective gear. This can lead to a reduction in your settlement amount.

For example, if you are found to be 20% at fault for not wearing a helmet, your total compensation may be reduced by 20%. However, if the accident was caused by another driver’s negligence, you may still be eligible for significant compensation.

2. Impact on Personal Injury Protection (PIP) Benefits

Michigan is a no-fault insurance state, meaning that motorcyclists must carry Personal Injury Protection (PIP) insurance to cover medical expenses. However, unlike car drivers, motorcyclists are not automatically covered under PIP insurance unless they are struck by a vehicle with Michigan no-fault insurance.

If you are injured in a motorcycle accident while not wearing a helmet, the insurance company may challenge the severity of your injuries and reduce or deny benefits, arguing that proper helmet use could have mitigated your injuries.

3. Helmet Use and Liability in Lawsuits

Even though Michigan law permits certain riders to ride without helmets, juries may view helmetless riders as partially responsible for their injuries. This can influence their decision in awarding damages for pain and suffering. Insurance adjusters and defense attorneys will likely use the lack of a helmet as an argument to minimize payouts in personal injury claims.

Types of Compensation You Can Recover

Despite the challenges helmetless riders may face, they can still recover damages, including:

  • Medical Expenses: Hospital bills, surgeries, rehabilitation, and ongoing medical care.
  • Lost Wages: Compensation for time off work due to injury.
  • Pain and Suffering: Emotional distress and reduced quality of life.
  • Property Damage: Repair or replacement costs for the motorcycle.
  • Wrongful Death Damages: If a loved one dies in a motorcycle accident, the family may pursue compensation for funeral expenses and loss of companionship.

Why You Need a Motorcycle Accident Lawyer in Michigan

If you’ve been injured in a motorcycle crash, whether or not you were wearing a helmet, hiring an experienced motorcycle accident lawyer in Michigan is crucial. A skilled attorney can:

  • Investigate the accident: Collect evidence, interview witnesses, and reconstruct the scene.
  • Negotiate with insurance companies: Ensure you receive a fair settlement.
  • Challenge comparative negligence claims: Argue against attempts to reduce your compensation unfairly.
  • Represent you in court: If a fair settlement isn’t reached, your lawyer can take the case to trial.

Common Defenses Used by Insurance Companies

Insurance companies often use various tactics to limit their payout, including:

  • Arguing that the lack of a helmet contributed to head and neck injuries.
  • Blaming the motorcyclist for the accident (e.g., reckless driving, speeding, or lane splitting).
  • Questioning the extent of injuries and requiring excessive medical documentation.
  • Offering lowball settlements to close cases quickly.

An experienced lawyer will counter these tactics and ensure you receive the compensation you deserve.

Steps to Take After a Motorcycle Accident in Michigan

If you’re involved in a motorcycle accident, follow these steps to protect your legal rights:

  1. Seek Medical Attention: Even if injuries seem minor, get checked by a doctor.
  2. Report the Accident: File a police report and obtain a copy for your records.
  3. Gather Evidence: Take photos, collect witness statements, and preserve medical records.
  4. Contact a Lawyer: Consult with a motorcycle accident lawyer in Michigan to evaluate your case.
  5. Avoid Speaking to Insurance Adjusters Alone: Let your attorney handle negotiations.

Conclusion

Michigan’s helmet laws play a significant role in motorcycle accident claims. While wearing a helmet is not legally required for all riders, it can impact the compensation you receive in an injury case. If you or a loved one has been injured in a motorcycle crash, hiring a knowledgeable attorney is essential.
